newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan delays exchanges with China - papers.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan delays exchanges with China - papers.

text.p: Taiwan's cabinet has decided to delay two exchange agreements with China following Beijing's pressure on the island's diplomatic allies, local media reported on Sunday.

The cabinet's Mainland Affairs Council proposed to the cabinet last year that more government officials, including the governor and mayors, be permitted to visit the mainland and that Chinese reporters be allowed to stay in Taiwan for up to two years.
But the cabinet, which has the final say, had decided to postpone the exchanges, council chairman Chang King-yuh was quoted by the China Times newspaper as saying.
"As communist China continues to suppress us overseas... the cabinet decided to postpone the opening on the two policies," Chang said over the weekend.
"It's not the cabinet will not put the two items into practice but that the timing of the opening needs more consideration," he said.
Taiwan and China have been rivals since the end of a civil war in 1949. Beijing, which has regarded Taiwan as a renegade province, has since tried to push the island into international isolation.

A political thaw starting in the late 1980s promoted active exchanges between the two sides but after Pretoria's late 1996 announcement that it would switch ties to Beijing from Taipei in 1997, the council said it would freeze further major exchanges with the mainland.
South Africa is the biggest of Taiwan's only 30 diplomatic allies.
On Friday China vetoed a resolution to send 155 United Nations' peacekeepers to Guatemala because of the Central American country's "erroneous position" in supporting Taiwan.
It was the first time Beijing had used its veto power in enarly 24 years.
Guatemala recognises Taipei instead of Beijing.

Although technical-level talks between the two rivals have been suspended by an angry Beijing, Chang was quoted by the United Daily News newspaper as saying that Taiwan would not rule out possibilities of discussing "political issues" in the future.
